display.title: Nottingham Monthly Temperatures
display.subtitle: Explore monthly temperature seasonality and forecast the next 12 months with governed univariate forecasting.
display.problem_summary_body: This dataset contains 240 monthly average air-temperature observations recorded at Nottingham Castle from 1920 through 1939. Atlas treats the series as a univariate forecasting problem: using the governed monthly history, the model forecasts the next 12 monthly temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit. Evaluation preserves temporal order through expanding-window backtesting and a final 1939 holdout.

home_card.short_description: Explore 20 years of Nottingham monthly average air temperatures and a governed univariate forecasting model that predicts the next 12 months in degrees Fahrenheit.

documentation.content:
# Nottingham Monthly Temperatures

This dataset presents a governed **univariate time-series forecasting** study of monthly average air temperatures recorded at Nottingham Castle from 1920 through 1939.

The objective is not only to produce a 12-month forecast, but to document the temporal structure of the series, preserve forecasting-specific evaluation discipline, compare candidate forecasting specifications against meaningful baselines, and evaluate one frozen model on a prospectively sealed final holdout.

## Dataset overview

The source is the classic `datasets::nottem` monthly temperature series distributed with R and acquired by the companion study through `statsmodels.datasets.get_rdataset`.

| Item | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Monthly observations | 240 |
| Coverage | `1920-01` → `1939-12` |
| Target | `temperature` |
| Target unit | degrees Fahrenheit (°F) |
| Frequency | monthly |
| Source exogenous predictors | none |
| Forecast horizon | 12 months |
| Problem type | Univariate forecasting |
| Scientific reference | `datasets::nottem` |

The canonical forecasting series contains only a time index and one endogenous numerical target.

The source transport representation is reconstructed as a monthly period index before forecasting analysis. The source time coordinate is not treated as an ordinary tabular predictive feature, and there are no external regressors or exogenous predictors in this study.

## Forecasting question

The analysis investigates three related questions:

1. **What temporal structure is present in Nottingham monthly temperatures?**
2. **Can a forecasting specification produce reliable 12-month forecasts beyond a seasonal-naive reference under temporally ordered backtesting?**
3. **How does the frozen selected model perform on the final 1939 holdout after model development is complete?**

Forecasting differs fundamentally from shuffled tabular prediction because observations are ordered in time and future values must remain unavailable at each forecast origin.

Random train/test shuffling or ordinary K-fold evaluation would therefore be inappropriate for this problem.

## Data quality and temporal preparation

The canonical series contains 240 consecutive monthly observations.

The companion study found:

* no missing canonical months;
* no duplicated canonical periods;
* no missing target values;
* no non-finite temperature values;
* no source exogenous predictors;
* no point anomalies meeting the predefined robust intervention threshold;
* no evidence requiring row deletion, interpolation, clipping, winsorization, or synthetic filling.

Preparation therefore preserves the observed monthly temperature series on its original Fahrenheit scale.

No generic logarithmic transformation, Box–Cox transformation, global scaling, full-series detrending, globally fitted decomposition, or mandatory differencing policy is applied before forecasting.

The series is divided along a temporal boundary:

| Scope | Range | Observations | Purpose |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Development | `1920-01` → `1938-12` | 228 | Backtesting and final model fitting |
| Final holdout | `1939-01` → `1939-12` | 12 | One-time final evaluation |

The final forecast origin is `1938-12`.

From the preparation stage onward, the 1939 holdout is excluded from model fitting, candidate comparison, metric-driven selection, retuning, and adjustment before its one-time final evaluation.

## Historical temperature evolution

The full historical record shows a pronounced repeating annual temperature cycle together with smaller long-run level movement.

Across the 240 observations, the companion study reports:

| Statistic | Temperature |
| --- | ---: |
| Mean | approximately 49.04 °F |
| Median | 47.35 °F |
| Minimum | 31.3 °F |
| Maximum | 66.5 °F |

![Monthly Nottingham temperature evolution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-nottingham-monthly-temperatures/main/docs/images/nottem_temperature_evolution.png)

The later years are modestly warmer on average than the earliest years in this record, but the long-run movement is much smaller than the recurring within-year seasonal variation.

The descriptive annual-mean slope is approximately `0.057 °F` per year, while the mean temperature during `1935–1939` is approximately `0.76 °F` above the mean during `1920–1924`.

These observations motivate consideration of a trend component, but they do not establish a causal climate trend or independently determine the final forecasting model.

## Seasonal structure

Seasonality is the dominant systematic pattern in the series.

Across development history, temperatures are lowest on average during winter and highest during summer. July has the highest cross-year calendar-month mean, while February has the lowest.

The exploratory calendar-month mean range is approximately **22.71 °F**.

![Calendar-month Nottingham temperature profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-nottingham-monthly-temperatures/main/docs/images/nottem_calendar_month_profile.png)

The companion study's STL diagnostics estimate seasonal strength at approximately `0.960`, substantially greater than the corresponding trend-strength estimate of approximately `0.241`.

![STL decomposition of the Nottingham monthly temperature series](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-nottingham-monthly-temperatures/main/docs/images/nottem_stl_decomposition.png)

This strong annual structure is why a 12-month seasonal-naive forecast is the primary baseline rather than a simple global mean prediction.

## Target distribution and dependence diagnostics

The marginal distribution of monthly temperatures summarizes the values observed across all seasons, but it should not be interpreted independently from time because each observation belongs to a recurring calendar position.

![Distribution of Nottingham monthly average temperatures](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-nottingham-monthly-temperatures/main/docs/images/nottem_target_distribution.png)

Autocorrelation also reflects the annual cycle.

The strongest observed absolute autocorrelation within 36 months occurs at lag 12, at approximately `0.884` on the complete series and approximately `0.886` within the development history.

![Autocorrelation diagnostics for Nottingham monthly temperatures](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-nottingham-monthly-temperatures/main/docs/images/nottem_autocorrelation.png)

Short-lag dependence is also substantial.

These diagnostics support explicit temporal modeling, but exploratory decomposition and autocorrelation results are not reused as globally fitted future-aware preprocessing inputs.

## Temporally ordered backtesting

Model development uses an **expanding-window** evaluation design rather than random resampling.

| Backtesting property | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Initial training history | 120 months |
| Forecast horizon per fold | 12 months |
| Origin step | 12 months |
| Backtesting folds | 9 |
| Validation years | 1930 → 1938 |
| Total out-of-sample forecasts per complete specification | 108 |

Each fold:

1. fits the candidate using only observations available up to that forecast origin;
2. produces all 12 future monthly forecasts without consulting validation targets;
3. evaluates those 12 forecasts against the next calendar year; and
4. expands the training history before the next origin.

Validation windows do not overlap, no fold reaches the 1939 final holdout, and future target values are never fed back within a fold.

This structure protects the evaluation from temporal leakage while testing the actual multi-step forecasting behavior required by the problem.

## Forecasting metrics

The governed forecasting evaluation uses:

* **MAE** as the primary metric;
* **RMSE** as a secondary metric;
* **Seasonal MASE(12)** as a scale-free secondary metric;
* horizon-wise forecast error as diagnostic evidence.

`MAPE` and `sMAPE` are deliberately excluded.

Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit has an arbitrary zero point, so percentage-of-observed-value errors do not have a stable physical interpretation for this target.

### MAE

Mean Absolute Error reports the average absolute forecast error in the original temperature unit.

**Lower values are better.**

Because MAE remains in degrees Fahrenheit, it is the most directly interpretable primary metric for this study.

### RMSE

Root Mean Squared Error also reports error on the Fahrenheit scale but gives greater weight to larger misses.

**Lower values are better.**

RMSE complements MAE rather than replacing it.

### Seasonal MASE(12)

Seasonal Mean Absolute Scaled Error compares forecast error with the scale of a 12-month seasonal-naive reference derived from the available training history.

A value below `1.0` indicates error smaller than the seasonal-naive scale represented by that denominator.

**Lower values are better.**

## Forecasting baselines

Two simple forecasting references are evaluated:

| Baseline | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| `seasonal_naive_12` | Forecast each month using the observation from the same month one year earlier |
| `naive_last_value` | Forecast every horizon using the final observed value at the forecast origin |

`seasonal_naive_12` is the primary benchmark because the dataset has strong annual seasonality.

A candidate model should therefore demonstrate useful forecasting skill beyond simply repeating last year's seasonal pattern.

## Model selection evidence

The companion scientific study evaluates two baselines and eight learned forecasting specifications under the frozen expanding-window schedule.

The strongest eligible specifications are tightly grouped:

| Forecasting specification | Backtesting MAE ↓ | RMSE ↓ | Seasonal MASE(12) ↓ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Deterministic Seasonal-Trend OLS** | **1.8394** | 2.3208 | **0.6570** |
| Holt-Winters additive, no trend | 1.8501 | 2.3385 | 0.6608 |
| SARIMA `(1,0,0)(0,1,1,12)` | 1.8523 | **2.3052** | 0.6617 |
| Holt-Winters additive, damped trend | 1.8539 | 2.3425 | 0.6621 |
| Holt-Winters additive trend | 1.8577 | 2.3439 | 0.6635 |
| Seasonal naive 12 | 2.6380 | 3.3389 | 0.9417 |
| Naive last value | 10.5639 | 13.2678 | 3.7707 |

![Backtesting MAE comparison across forecasting specifications](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-nottingham-monthly-temperatures/main/docs/images/nottem_model_selection_mae.png)

The frozen practical-tie tolerance is `0.05 °F` on pooled MAE.

Five learned candidates fall within that tolerance of the best raw MAE. The deterministic tie-break sequence then considers:

1. pooled Seasonal MASE;
2. pooled RMSE;
3. fold-to-fold MAE standard deviation;
4. long-horizon MAE across horizons 7–12;
5. model complexity rank;
6. candidate identifier.

Under this policy, `seasonal_trend_ols` is selected.

Its backtesting MAE improves on `seasonal_naive_12` by approximately **0.7985 °F**, corresponding to approximately **30.3%** relative improvement in MAE.

The companion study performs this model-selection analysis. The active Atlas release does **not** rerun unrestricted model search: its governed execution contract freezes the selected family and configuration as a fixed model specification.

## Selected forecasting model

The active model family is:

`deterministic_seasonal_trend_ols`

The fitted specification contains:

* an intercept;
* a linear time trend;
* additive monthly seasonal indicators;
* a seasonal period of 12 months;
* January as the reference seasonal position.

The model therefore represents the series as a combination of gradual time movement and a stable recurring calendar-month pattern.

It does not use exogenous predictors.

The active Atlas training policy reconstructs this fixed configuration, refits it independently inside each backtesting fold for evaluation, fits the final model on the complete development history, and freezes the model before opening the final holdout.

## Active Atlas release evaluation

The active Atlas release is:

`release-20260828t211723z`

The final model is fitted on:

```text
1920-01 → 1938-12
228 monthly observations
```

The frozen model is then evaluated exactly once on:

```text
1939-01 → 1939-12
12 monthly observations
```

The active release reports:

| Metric | Final 1939 holdout |
| --- | ---: |
| **MAE ↓** | **1.5266 °F** |
| RMSE ↓ | **1.8600 °F** |
| Seasonal MASE(12) ↓ | **0.5555** |

The final metrics are numerically better than the pooled backtesting metrics for this single 12-month holdout, but this should be interpreted only as observed evidence for 1939.

A single final year does not establish that future years will always be easier to forecast or that the final-holdout error is a better estimate than the multi-origin backtesting evidence.

## Final 1939 forecast versus observed temperatures

The active Atlas release carries governed forecast-versus-actual evidence for every month in the final holdout.

![Final 1939 Nottingham forecast versus observed temperature](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-nottingham-monthly-temperatures/main/docs/images/nottem_final_forecast.png)

The forecast preserves the broad seasonal shape of the observed 1939 series, including the winter low-temperature region, the rise into summer, and the decline toward year end.

The largest absolute misses in the active final holdout occur around October and November, while several spring and early-summer months are forecast more closely.

This variation is expected in a multi-step forecast and is one reason aggregate metrics should be interpreted together with forecast-versus-actual evidence rather than in isolation.

## Understanding the highlighted metrics

### MAE — 1.5266 °F

The final-holdout MAE means that the 12 monthly forecasts differ from the observed 1939 temperatures by approximately **1.53 °F on average**, ignoring error direction.

MAE is the primary governed metric and the highlighted forecasting score in Atlas.

**Lower values are better.**

### RMSE — 1.8600 °F

RMSE gives additional weight to larger monthly errors.

The fact that RMSE is higher than MAE is expected because the two metrics aggregate errors differently and should not be compared as if the numerically smaller metric were automatically superior.

**Lower values are better.**

### Seasonal MASE(12) — 0.5555

Seasonal MASE expresses the forecast error relative to a seasonal-naive error scale based on a 12-month seasonal period.

A value of approximately `0.5555` is below `1.0`, indicating that the frozen model's final-holdout absolute error is favorable relative to the seasonal-naive scaling reference used by the governed evaluation.

**Lower values are better.**

## Backtesting diagnostics across forecast origins

The active Atlas release also preserves MAE for each of the nine expanding-window forecast origins.

The pooled backtesting MAE is approximately `1.8394 °F`, but performance varies between origins.

The lowest fold MAE is approximately `1.3961 °F`, while the highest is approximately `2.8618 °F`.

This variability is useful evidence because a forecasting model can perform differently across calendar years even when the evaluation geometry remains unchanged.

Atlas therefore presents multi-origin evidence rather than relying only on one final score.

## Horizon-wise forecasting diagnostics

The 12-month horizon is also evaluated by forecast step across all nine backtesting origins.

Horizon-wise MAE is not monotonic: error does not simply increase one month at a time as the forecast moves farther into the future.

In the active release, the lowest backtesting MAE occurs around horizons 4 and 5, while horizon 12 has the highest horizon-wise MAE among the 12 steps.

This diagnostic should be interpreted as a summary across nine historical forecast origins, not as the error of the single 1939 forecast shown in the final holdout chart.

It helps reveal whether certain seasonal positions or forecast distances are consistently more difficult than others.

## Forecasting presentation in Atlas

The current Atlas release presents Nottingham as an **evaluation-oriented forecasting experience**.

The public dataset surface emphasizes:

* the governed final 1939 forecast versus observed values;
* final-holdout MAE, RMSE, and Seasonal MASE;
* expanding-window backtesting evidence;
* metric behavior across forecast origins;
* horizon-wise diagnostics;
* the selected deterministic seasonal-trend model.

The current public contract explicitly marks interactive public prediction as:

```text
not_applicable
```

This is intentional for the active release.

The frozen `DeterministicSeasonalTrendOLS` coefficients are not updated by user-supplied historical temperature values, and the governed predictive-interaction policy declares that those target values do not affect the forecast produced by this model.

Atlas therefore does not present an interactive Inference tab for this release merely to collect historical values that would not modify the model's forecast.

This decision is specific to the current governed predictive-interaction semantics and should not be generalized to every future univariate forecasting model. A future model whose historical values form genuine prediction context may legitimately expose a different public interaction contract while still using the same broader forecasting capability.

## What this dataset demonstrates

Nottingham Monthly Temperatures extends Atlas into native univariate forecasting.

The dataset demonstrates:

* temporal rather than shuffled evaluation geometry;
* a canonical time index and one endogenous numerical target;
* monthly-frequency governance;
* fixed multi-step forecast horizons;
* expanding-window backtesting;
* leakage-safe fold-local fitting;
* seasonal-naive and last-value forecasting baselines;
* MAE-driven model selection evidence;
* seasonal MASE evaluation;
* horizon-wise forecasting diagnostics;
* deterministic practical-tie model selection in the companion study;
* fixed-model reproduction inside Atlas rather than unrestricted AutoML;
* one-time final-holdout opening after model freeze;
* ordered forecast-series result semantics;
* forecast-versus-actual analytical evidence;
* capability-driven suppression of public prediction when predictive interaction is not meaningful for the active model.

It therefore demonstrates that Atlas can represent predictive problems whose output is an ordered future series rather than a class label or single scalar regression estimate.

## Limitations

Several important boundaries remain:

* the complete source contains only 240 monthly observations, corresponding to 20 annual cycles;
* model development uses 228 observations and the final holdout contains only 12 observations;
* the 1939 holdout is prospectively sealed from Notebook 02 onward, but it is **not exploration-blind** because the initial retrospective exploration inspected the complete 1920–1939 source before the final model-development boundary was frozen;
* the final holdout is only one calendar year and does not establish performance under future regime changes;
* no exogenous climate, atmospheric, geographic, or measurement variables are available to the model;
* the deterministic seasonal-trend specification assumes a stable recurring monthly seasonal structure plus a linear time component;
* exploratory autocorrelation, STL decomposition, stationarity tests, and trend summaries do not prove a causal data-generating mechanism;
* no calibrated forecast interval or probabilistic uncertainty distribution is presented by the active Atlas release;
* the study does not establish performance under structural climate change, measurement-system changes, missing months, revised source values, or other forms of distribution shift;
* no production drift monitoring, scheduled retraining policy, or operational forecasting guarantee is established;
* the current absence of public interactive prediction is a governed property of this release, not a universal restriction on univariate forecasting in Atlas.

## Responsible interpretation

The evidence supports the following conclusion:

> Nottingham Monthly Temperatures is a small, clean, strongly seasonal monthly series in which annual seasonality dominates the systematic structure. Under nine-fold expanding-window backtesting, the deterministic seasonal-trend OLS specification achieves a pooled MAE of approximately 1.8394 °F and improves MAE by about 30.3% relative to the seasonal-naive reference. The active Atlas release freezes that governed model configuration before opening the 1939 final holdout and achieves a final MAE of approximately 1.5266 °F, RMSE of approximately 1.8600 °F, and Seasonal MASE of approximately 0.5555.

The Atlas presentation should therefore be interpreted as an educational demonstration of governed multi-step time-series forecasting, temporal evaluation, and forecast evidence.

The historical relationships and observed forecasting performance do not establish causal climate effects, guaranteed future accuracy, or operational forecasting validity outside the documented dataset and evaluation design.
